title: What an extension tells you
objectives: Recognise common file types from their extension
Explain why renaming a file does not convert it
Find hidden files and name files so they sort and type cleanly

screens.prose: This is Ana's `Downloads` folder. Every name ends with a dot and a few letters.
screens.question: Tap the names of the two pictures.

hints.text: Look at the letters after the dot. Which ones have you seen on photos?
One picture is the second largest file here.
`.png` and `.jpg` are picture formats: `chart.png` and `photo.jpg`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the letters after the dot in each name.

byKey.pdf: A PDF can contain pictures, but it is a document of pages. The two picture files end in `.png` and `.jpg`.
byKey.r7c0: A PDF can contain pictures, but it is a document of pages.
byKey.r4c0: `.xlsx` is an Excel workbook: tables, not a picture.

explain.text: You read the ending of each name: `.png` and `.jpg` mean pictures. You did not need to open anything. The ending told you what kind of file it was.

screens.prose: Here is what each file looks like when forced open in a plain text editor. Some show readable words. Others show symbol soup, because they are not stored as text.

columns: First characters, opened in a text editor

screens.question: Tap the names of every file stored as readable text.

hints.text: Read the right-hand column. Could a person read it?
This one is readable, even though it holds numbers.

feedback.correct: The `.csv`, `.py`, `.txt` and `.md` files are plain text.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick every name whose right-hand column reads as normal characters.

byKey.no-csv: You left out `prices.csv`. A CSV is a table written as plain text, commas between values.
byKey.xlsx: You included `results.xlsx`. Excel packs its tables into a compressed format, so a text editor shows symbols.
byKey.r2c0: A PNG stores pixels, not characters, so it shows symbol soup.
byKey.r7c0: A PDF starts with a readable tag, then turns to symbols. It is not plain text.

explain.text: Four files show readable text: the CSV, the Python script, the text note and the Markdown file. The others store pixels or packed data. The ending of each name predicted which was which.

screens.prose: The letters after the last dot in a name are the file's **extension**. It is a label saying how the inside is written, so programs know how to read it.

columns: First characters, opened in a text editor

screens.question: Match each extension to what is inside.

hints.text: Use the inside column: which file starts `date,close`, which `import csv`, which `#`?
The Markdown file starts with a heading mark.
`.csv`: table as text. `.py`: Python code. `.md`: notes with headings. `.png`: picture.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each extension to the file's inside in the table.

byKey.md: `.md` is Markdown: plain-text notes where `#` marks a heading.
byKey.csv: `.csv` means comma-separated values: a table, row by row, as text.
byKey.py: `.py` holds Python code. Its first line here is `import csv`.

explain.text: You matched each extension to what the file holds. CSV stands for comma-separated values. These four are the extensions you will meet most in this course.

screens.prose: An extension says how the inside is written, not which program must open it. `prices.csv` is a plain-text table.

columns: First characters, opened in a text editor

screens.question: Select all that apply: which of these can open `prices.csv` and show its numbers?

options.why: You matched by habit rather than content. An image viewer expects pixels; a CSV holds characters.

hints.text: The inside is ordinary characters. Which programs read characters?
Anything that reads text can read a CSV: an editor, a spreadsheet, a script. An image viewer reads pixels.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which programs can read plain characters.

byKey.sheet: A spreadsheet reads a CSV and lays it out in a grid.
byKey.python: Python reads text files, and CSVs are text files.
byKey.editor: A text editor shows any plain-text file, a CSV included.

explain.text: A CSV is plain text, so anything that reads text can open it. Your computer just picks a default program for each extension. You can always choose another.

screens.prose: This table lists everything in Ana's `project` folder. Her normal folder view shows only four items: `data`, `notes`, `README.md` and `src`.

state.caption: Normal view shows: data, notes, README.md, src

screens.question: Tap the names the normal view hides.

hints.text: Compare the table with the four names in the caption.
Look at the first character of these two.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the names that are in the table but missing from the caption.

byKey.r4c0: `README.md` has a dot inside its name, and it is shown. Only a dot at the very start hides a file.

explain.text: Both hidden names start with a dot. A leading dot marks a **hidden file**, usually settings. To see them: Cmd Shift . in macOS Finder, View then Hidden items in Windows, or `ls -a` in a terminal.

screens.prose: Ana's broker exports a file called `spx.2024.daily.csv`. The diagram splits the name at each dot.
screens.question: What is the file's extension?

options.why: You took everything after the first dot. The extension is only what follows the last dot.
That is the start of the name. The extension is at the end.

options.text: It has none: a name may hold only one dot
options.why: Names may hold many dots. Only the last one starts the extension.

hints.text: Which dot comes last?
This is the last dot.
After the last dot comes `csv`, so the extension is `.csv`.

feedback.correct: Only the part after the last dot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the last dot in the name.

explain.text: Dots inside a name are just characters. Only the last one starts the extension. So this is a CSV named `spx.2024.daily`.

screens.prose: Ana's script reads CSV files. Her results are in `results.xlsx`, so she renames the file to `results.csv` and runs the script.

columns: First characters, opened in a text editor

screens.question: What happens?

options.text: The script fails or reads nonsense: the inside is still Excel's packed format.
The script reads the table, because the name now ends in `.csv`.
options.why: You treated the extension as the contents. Renaming changed the label only; the inside is the same bytes.

options.text: The file is converted to CSV, but loses its colours and formulas.
options.why: You expected renaming to convert. Converting needs Excel's Save As, choosing CSV.

hints.text: Compare the two rows of the table.
The insides are identical.
Renaming changes the name only. The bytes are still an Excel workbook.

feedback.correct: The inside did not change, so the script cannot read it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what renaming did to the inside.

byKey.works: You treated the extension as the contents. Renaming relabelled the same packed bytes. Use Save As, then choose CSV.

explain.text: Both rows start with the same symbols: renaming did not touch the inside. It only made the label lie. To get a real CSV, open the workbook and use Save As with the CSV format.

screens.prose: Every name you read had two parts. The extension starts at the last dot and labels how the inside is written: $$\underbrace{\texttt{spx.2024.daily}}_{\text{name}}\underbrace{\texttt{.csv}}_{\text{extension}}$$ A dot at the very start hides the file instead.
screens.question: Which of these changes what is inside a file?

options.text: Using Save As in Excel and choosing CSV

options.why: Renaming changes the label only. You saw the inside stay the same.

options.text: Renaming it to start with a dot
options.why: A leading dot hides the file from the normal view. The inside is untouched.

hints.text: Which action writes the data out again in a new format?
Only Save As rewrites the contents. The other two only rename.

feedback.correct: Only a real conversion rewrites the inside.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A rename changes the name and nothing else.

explain.text: Renaming, including adding a leading dot, never changes the inside. A program such as Excel must rewrite the data in the new format. The extension should then match what was written.

screens.prose: Python's `sorted()` and the terminal's `ls` compare names one character at a time, from the left. Ana saved one result file per test run.
screens.question: Put the names in the order those tools sort them, first at the top.

hints.text: Compare `run-10.csv` and `run-2.csv` character by character.
Both start `run-`. Next is `1` against `2`, and `1` comes first. So `run-10.csv` sorts before `run-2.csv`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare one character at a time, not whole numbers.

explain.text: Character by character, `1` beats `2`, so run 10 lands between runs 1 and 2. Padding with zeros fixes it: `run-01.csv` to `run-10.csv` sort in order. Dates need the same care.

screens.prose: Ana's script on a Linux server opens `data/Prices.csv`. The file on the server is called `data/prices.csv`.
screens.question: What happens?

options.text: File not found: on Linux `P` and `p` are different letters in a name.
It opens: names ignore capital letters.
options.why: That is true by default on Windows and macOS, so it may have worked on your laptop. Linux servers treat case as different.

options.text: The server renames the file to match.
options.why: Nothing renames files on your behalf. The script just asks for a path that does not exist.

hints.text: Is `Prices` the same text as `prices`, letter for letter?
On Linux names are case-sensitive, so these are two different names.

feedback.correct: Different case, different name on Linux.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two names letter for letter.

explain.text: Linux sees two different names, so the script fails there while working on a laptop. Using only lower case removes the problem. Spaces cause similar trouble in the terminal, so join words with hyphens: `daily-prices.csv`.

screens.prose: Ana exports month-end prices each month, naming each file by day, month, year. Sorted by name, her folder lists them like this. The dates run out of order.
screens.question: Which naming scheme makes the name order the same as the date order?

options.why: That is the scheme in the table. It sorts by day of the month first.
Month names sort alphabetically: apr, aug, dec, feb. That is not date order.
Without the zero, month 10 sorts before month 2, as `run-10` did.

hints.text: Character by character, the leftmost part counts most. Which part of a date should count most?
Here the day decides the order.
Put the year first, then a two-digit month, then a two-digit day: YYYY-MM-DD.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The largest unit must come first, with every part padded to a fixed width.

byKey.dmy: You kept the day first. Character by character, the day then decides the order, as the table shows.

explain.text: With the year first and every part padded, sorting by name is sorting by date. That is the ISO 8601 date format, YYYY-MM-DD. Use it in every file name in this course.

ideas: The extension, after the last dot, labels how the inside is written: `.csv`, `.py` and `.md` are plain text; `.png` and `.xlsx` are not.
A name that starts with a dot is hidden from the normal view. `ls -a` and your file browser's settings show it.
Name files in lower case, with hyphens for spaces and dates as YYYY-MM-DD. They then work everywhere and sort in date order.

formula.name: A file name
formula.note: The extension starts at the last dot.

summary.trap: Renaming `results.xlsx` to `results.csv` does not convert it. Use Save As and choose CSV.

options.why: You started at the first dot. The extension follows the last dot.
A name may hold any number of dots. The last one starts the extension.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the last dot.

explain.text: The last dot is just before `csv`. So the file is a CSV named `trades.2024-06`.

quiz.question: Which of them does the normal folder view hide?

options.why: That name has a dot inside, not at the start. Only a leading dot hides a file.

options.text: All three, since they all contain a dot
options.why: Every name with an extension has a dot. Only a dot at the very start hides it.

feedback.correct: Only the name starting with a dot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first character of each name.

explain.text: `.env` starts with a dot, so it is hidden. The other two have dots inside their names, which hide nothing.

quiz.prose: Ana is naming an export of S&P 500 closes for 31 March 2025.
quiz.question: Which name follows all of this course's naming rules?

options.why: The date is right, but capitals and spaces cause trouble on Linux and in the terminal.
Day first sorts by day of the month. Put the year first.
Without the zero, month 3 sorts after month 10. Pad the month to two digits.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check case, spaces and the date order.

explain.text: Lower case and hyphens work on every system and in the terminal. YYYY-MM-DD with two-digit months and days sorts in date order.

quiz.prose: Ana renames `chart.png` to `chart.csv` and opens it in a text editor.
quiz.question: What does she see?

options.text: Symbol soup: the inside is still a picture's pixels.
The chart's numbers as a table.
options.why: You expected the rename to convert the picture. Renaming leaves the bytes as they were.

options.text: An empty file: renaming wiped it.
options.why: Renaming never deletes contents. The bytes are untouched.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Renaming changes the name only.

explain.text: The file still holds PNG pixel data. Only its label now claims CSV. A picture cannot become a table by renaming.
